newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals-Vanadium up on talk of China closure.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals-Vanadium up on talk of China closure.

text.p: Ferro-vanadium prices have firmed further amid talks of declining production in China, one of the world's major producers, due to a shortage of vanadium slabs, traders said on Tuesday.
"There's a gap between demand and supply. Ferro-vanadium prices will exceed $20 (per kg) in the near future," said a trader at one of Japan's major trading houses.
Traders in Tokyo said Chinese offers were drying up as Panzhihua Iron and Steel (Group) Corp, the country's sole supplier of vanadium slabs, appeared to have closed for maintainance.
But in China, an official at Panzhihua's research department told Reuters the company had not stopped production of vanadium slab, the raw material for ferro vanadium.
"We never planned to stop production of vanadium slab," he said. "Demand (for vanadium slabs) exceeds supply now."
"Our output of vanadium slab in 1996 was 83,334 tonnes, up from around 52,000 tonnes in 1995," he said. "Most of that volume is usually exported."
Japanese traders said ferro-vanadium was quoted around $19-20 per kg, while the price of vanadium slab climbed to above $4 per pound.
In China, local prices for the minor metal, used for special steel, have risen in the past few months and are now indicated at $19.50/20.00 per kg on a cost and freight (C&F) basis, an official said.

"China's total output of ferro-vanadium is around 100,000 tonnes a year, though output in 1996 was less than that," the official at Panzhihua's affiliated trading company said by telephone from western Sichuan province.
He also said the company accounted for 87 percent of China's total output and that 70 to 80 percent of Panzhihua's output was exported.
In the Asian cobalt market, prices continued to firm, with high-grade cobalt quoted at $23-24 per pound and low-grade cobalt at $19-20, traders said.

End-users started to buy the metal as their hopes of lower prices were dashed, despite the expected resumption of sales by the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) in August and the end of a strike at a plant of Canada's Inco Ltd, they said.

"Stocks at large users and traders are running low. U.S. demand for super-alloy as well as Japanese demand for batteries is strong," said one trader in Tokyo. "The price may go up by another dollar or two."
Keen buying interest from China had helped push cobalt prices up from recent dips, a trader in Bejing added.
Cobalt ingots were indicated at $19.50/20.50 basis cost and freight (C&F) Chinese ports, he said.
The magnesium market remained quiet, with Chinese special high-grade (SHG) quoted at $2,400-2,500 per tonne.
Yet traders in Tokyo said demand from beverage can makers might rise later this quarter if the current heat wave continued to grip Japan.
"We say one sunny day means 20 tonnes of additional magnesium," said one trader.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544 -- Nao Nakanishi, Tokyo Newsroom (813) 3432-6179
